name: The Right to an Explanation
title: The Right to an Explanation
answer: The right to an explanation is a legal and policy claim that a person affected by an automated decision can obtain meaningful information about how that decision was reached. It sits within emerging legal frameworks and is often discussed alongside data protection, administrative law, consumer protection, and employment law. The right is not a single global rule, and its strength, triggers, and exceptions vary by jurisdiction and by the type of decision. In practice it usually covers the logic involved, the main factors, and the consequences, rather than the full source code or every internal weight. It is part of a broader movement to make automated systems contestable and accountable.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: The right to an explanation is a legal and policy claim that a person affected by an automated decision can obtain meaningful information about how that decision was reached. It sits within emerging legal frameworks and is often discussed alongside data protection, administrative law, consumer protection, and employment law. The right is not a single global rule, and its strength, triggers, and exceptions vary by jurisdiction and by the type of decision. In practice it usually covers the logic involved, the main factors, and the consequences, rather than the full source code or every internal weight. It is part of a broader movement to make automated systems contestable and accountable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The right runs on legal and organizational infrastructure rather than on a single technology. It depends on data subject access request workflows, decision logs, model documentation, version control, and records of human review. Compliance teams, data protection officers, regulators, and courts are the main actors who interpret and enforce it. Technical teams supply the evidence, such as training data summaries, feature lists, and audit trails, that makes an explanation possible after the fact. Without reliable logging and documentation, an organization cannot reconstruct why a particular output occurred.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a mix of legal analysis and technical investigation. A practitioner maps the relevant legal standard, identifies the automated decision at issue, and gathers records from the teams that built or operate the system. They then translate the system's logic into plain language, covering the data used, the main factors, and the significance of the outcome. The explanation may be delivered in a written response, a hearing, or a regulatory filing, and it is often tested by whether a reasonable person can understand and challenge the result. This is not the same as disclosing proprietary code or model weights, and trade secret protections usually shape what can be said.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk meet here because an explanation can conflict with privacy, security, intellectual property, and trade secret interests. Provenance matters, since the quality of an explanation depends on knowing where data came from, how a model was trained, and whether it has changed since the decision. Regulators and courts balance the individual's need for reasons against the organization's interest in protecting confidential methods. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages and 29 AI case law precedents, which show how explanation duties are being interpreted across different settings. Poor or generic explanations create legal risk, while overly detailed disclosures can expose systems to misuse or copying.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The right to an explanation is likely to expand as AI regulation grows. The site tracks 6979 state AI bills, and some of those proposals include notice, explanation, or appeal rights for automated decisions. Courts and regulators may clarify how much detail is enough and when a human review is required. Expect more guidance on documentation, audit trails, and standardized explanations, along with continued divergence between jurisdictions. The practical direction is toward explanations that are timely, specific, and connected to a real path for contesting the decision.
